tldr: The authors propose MorphIK, a generative model that solves inverse kinematics (IK) with high precision for 6- to 9-DoF robots it has never seen during training, simply by taking geometric information extracted from a URDF as input.
hero_caption: Overall system overview of MorphIK. Geometric tokens for each joint and the target pose are fed into a Transformer to produce a context vector, which then conditions a Flow-Matching head that generates joint configuration solutions from noise.
overview:
Moving a multi-joint robot's end-effector to a desired target pose via Inverse Kinematics (IK) is fundamental in robotics. For redundant robots with many degrees of freedom, multiple valid postures exist. In recent years, neural network approaches that can sample in parallel at high speed on GPUs and capture solution diversity (null space) have gained attention. However, conventional neural IK solvers faced a major barrier: they could only be trained specifically for a single robot. Whenever the arm configuration or dimensions changed, one had to recollect massive data and train a model from scratch.

To solve this, the authors developed MorphIK, a generalist foundation model that takes the robot's morphology itself as input and can solve IK even for robots seen for the first time. The key idea is to define a "canonical representation" that strips away geometric ambiguities from the robot's URDF and feed it into a Transformer as a sequence of tokens. Furthermore, by pairing this with Flow Matching, a fast and stable generative model, it generates joint angles that fulfill the specified target pose directly from noise. The training uses no real-world robot data at all; it relies entirely on synthetic data produced by forward kinematics (FK) on 400,000 procedurally generated random robots.

In evaluation experiments, the authors validated the model on 44 real-world robots with 6 to 9 degrees of freedom (such as UR, Franka, KUKA, etc.) never seen during training. As a result, raw model inference alone predicted poses with an accuracy of around 4% of total arm length (about 5 cm). Moreover, combining it with just 1 to 3 steps of traditional local optimization (Damped Least Squares: DLS) achieved ultra-high, sub-millimeter precision.
contributions: Defined a "canonical robot representation" that removes geometric ambiguities from robot URDFs, allowing consistent comparison and input across different arms.
Proposed a versatile architecture combining a Transformer and Flow Matching to simultaneously generate diverse IK solutions conditioned on robot morphology and target end-effector poses.
Built a fully self-supervised synthetic dataset of 400,000 procedurally generated random robots, achieving zero-shot generalization to real hardware without any real-world data.
Demonstrated practical utility and fast parallel inference, achieving ~5 cm precision out-of-the-box and sub-millimeter accuracy with just a few steps of post-processing DLS optimization.

sections.heading: Why move from single-robot training to "IK that solves any robot"?
sections.summary: While traditional neural IK solvers are fast and robust to singularities, being specialized to a single robot has been their biggest drawback. This work introduces MorphIK, a generalist model that directly solves IK from URDFs even for unseen 6–9 DoF arms.
sections.details:
Inverse kinematics (IK) is an unavoidable problem when operating robots, but when degrees of freedom increase and introduce redundancy, infinitely many solutions exist, making computation difficult. Recently, learning-based neural network approaches have gained traction over classical numerical optimization. Running batched inference on GPUs allows computing many solutions at once, and they are robust to singularities (postures where the Jacobian determinant becomes 0 and calculations fail). Generative models like Flow Matching and diffusion models naturally handle the one-to-many distribution where multiple joint configurations exist for a single target pose.

However, existing neural IK models had a critical flaw: they only worked on the specific single robot they were trained on. If link lengths changed slightly or if one switched to an arm from another manufacturer, massive datasets had to be collected and models retrained from scratch.

To address this, this paper proposes MorphIK. Instead of fixing the robot's structure, it tokenizes the geometry read from a URDF file and feeds it to the model as input. For training, it uses a large pool of procedurally generated random robots, producing unlimited data via self-supervised forward kinematics (FK). As a result, despite being trained without ever seeing real robots, it generalizes zero-shot to unknown real arms and reaches sub-millimeter precision with minimal correction using DLS (Damped Least Squares).

sections.heading: Numerical methods, genetic algorithms, and the evolution of neural IK
sections.summary: Against Jacobian-based methods like KDL and Trac-IK or optimization approaches like Bio-IK, neural methods offer advantages in parallelism and singularity avoidance. MorphIK expands generative IK—previously confined to single robots—to unknown, diverse robots.
sections.details:
Widely used traditional IK solvers like KDL and Trac-IK search for solutions using the Jacobian matrix that connects joint velocities to end-effector velocities. However, near singularities, velocities diverge to infinity, requiring workarounds like damping. On the other hand, genetic algorithms like Bio-IK do not rely on Jacobians and can handle flexible constraints, but they suffer from very high computational costs.

Neural approaches emerged to tackle these issues. They enable ultra-fast parallel inference on GPUs and can effectively explore the null space of redundant DoFs (the space where joints move without moving the end-effector). For instance, "IK-Flow" generated multimodal solutions using Normalizing Flows, and "CycleIK" trained GANs or MLPs with differentiable FK to minimize errors in task space.

However, most powerful recent methods—including "IKDiffuser" (handling multiple end-effectors) and "MimicIK" (Flow Matching for teleoperation IK)—remained single-robot models. Very few works, such as Generative Graphical IK using distance geometry graphs, have tackled multiple robots. MorphIK extends the generative capabilities of Flow Matching to morphological descriptors, achieving multi-robot IK that can generalize to diverse, unseen arms with a single model.

sections.heading: How to represent and solve unknown robots: representations and model design
sections.summary: The model tokenizes URDFs using a "canonical representation" that eliminates frame ambiguities, and combines a Transformer with Flow Matching to generate joint angles. To stabilize training, a differentiable FK loss evaluating predicted trajectory endpoints was introduced.
sections.details:
### III-A Canonical Robot Representation
When feeding robots into a model, using standard DH parameters or raw URDFs causes parameters to vary wildly depending on coordinate frame choices, even for identical arm shapes. Therefore, the authors devised a "canonical representation" that defines all joints as screw axes (rotation axes and points in space) in a single shared frame. By aligning the first joint axis with the $+z$-axis, picking the closest points between adjacent axes, and eliminating redundant rotations and axis flips through consistent rules, they produce a unique representation. Furthermore, scaling the total arm length to 1 provides scale invariance.

### III-B Dataset
Training uses 400,000 procedurally generated fictitious robots (100,000 for each class from 6 to 9 DoF). To mimic real robot structures, link lengths follow a Dirichlet distribution, with 35% of link lengths set to 0 to produce intersecting axes (spherical joints). Axis directions are sampled with structural proportions: parallel to the previous axis (25%), orthogonal (55%), or random (20%). Joint angles are sampled randomly, self-collisions are checked with simple capsules, and FK is solved on GPU to create training pairs. The generated robots have manipurability roughly 5 times lower and Jacobian condition numbers roughly 2 times higher than real robots, making them a harsh training dataset that is actually much harder to solve numerically than real hardware.

### III-C Model Architecture
The model consists of a Transformer backbone and a Flow-Matching head. Geometry tokens for each joint, a tool center point (TCP) token representing the rest pose, and a query token for the target pose are fed into the Transformer, which encodes morphology and target context via self-attention. This context vector is passed via AdaLN (Adaptive Layer Normalization) to the Flow-Matching head (MLP), which predicts joint velocity vectors $v_\theta$ from noise and integrates them to generate target joint angles.

### III-D Losses
In addition to the standard Flow-Matching mean squared error loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$, an FK loss measuring end-effector pose error directly was introduced. Exploiting the fact that the Flow-Matching velocity field is nearly straight, the endpoint joint configuration $\hat{q}$ is estimated in one step from the current state along the predicted velocity. Forward kinematics is then applied differentiably to compute position and orientation errors in Cartesian space. Because estimates are unstable early in the flow, a time gate weighting with $t^2$ toward the end of the process is applied, dramatically stabilizing training.

### III-E Training
The model was trained for 1,000,000 steps with a batch size of 2048 and a learning rate decaying from 5.4e-4 to 8e-6. The FK loss weight was set to 6 times the Flow-Matching loss. Inference is performed with 10 Euler integration steps on a single Nvidia RTX 5080 (16 GB VRAM).

sections.heading: How well can it solve unknown robots? Three evaluation scenarios
sections.summary: The evaluation assessed raw IK solver performance, effectiveness as an initial seed for DLS optimization, and fine-tuning capability as a foundation model for specific robots.
sections.details:
In the experiments, the authors designed three use cases to comprehensively evaluate MorphIK's capabilities:

- **Raw IK Solver**: Measuring error when using the generated solutions directly.
- **Seed Model for DLS**: Applying classical Jacobian-based local search (Damped Least Squares: DLS) for just 1 to 5 post-processing steps to test how much precision improves.
- **Foundation Model**: Comparing how much training cost is saved when fine-tuning the model for a specific robot compared to training from scratch.

Test targets included 800 unseen synthetic robots generated with the same procedural pipeline (200 per DoF class) and 44 real-world robot arms (6 to 7 DoF arms from UR, Franka, KUKA, Kinova, etc., plus 8 to 9 DoF arms created by attaching a Shadow Hand wrist joint). None of these real-world robots were seen during training.

sections.heading: Surprising generalization: sub-millimeter precision and rich null spaces on unseen real robots
sections.summary: The model achieved an average precision of about 5 cm on unseen real robots out-of-the-box, reaching sub-millimeter precision (under 0.1 mm) with just 3 steps of DLS. Additionally, leveraging generative modeling enabled rapid exploration of diverse configurations for the same target pose.
sections.details:
### Raw Model and DLS Correction Accuracy
At test time, 16 solutions were generated in parallel from Flow Matching and the best one was selected (Best of 16). On unseen synthetic robots, the raw model's average position error was 3.67% of total arm length, and rotation error was 2.84 degrees. On real robots, which are cleanly engineered by design, the model performed even better, showing strong raw results and massive benefits from DLS refinement.
On real robots, applying just a single step of DLS reduced average position error to around 0.5 cm (less than 0.6% of arm length) and rotation error to under 1 degree—nearly a 4x reduction. After 3 steps, the median error reached 0.01% of total arm length (sub-millimeter precision under 1 mm on typical arm sizes). Because the initial guess is accurate and far from singularities, local optimization converges remarkably fast.

### Trends Across Arms
Looking at individual real arms (Figure 5), Piper + Shadow Hand performed best with a 2.37% position error, while Comau e.DO + wrist showed 5.98%. Comparing arms with and without wrists, raw model error stayed nearly unchanged with or without a wrist. This is because errors in the base joints closest to the root have the largest effect on end-effector position. However, DLS convergence was faster for higher-DoF arms (8 to 9 DoF with wrists).

### V-A Null Space Modeling
Sampling 128 solutions for the same target pose tested how well the model covers different joint configurations. On real 7-DoF arms, it found an average of 42.8 valid solutions that differed by at least 0.25 rad from each other, and 80.5 on 9-DoF arms with wrists. Because it is a generative model that avoids Jacobian inversion, it proved capable of sampling vast null spaces in parallel instantly.

### V-B Finetuning
Eight real robots were chosen for single-robot fine-tuning. Remarkably, just 50 steps of additional training (about 1 second of wall-clock time) improved position error by ~30% and rotation error by 25%. While a model trained from scratch barely learned after 1,000 steps, pretrained MorphIK showed an overwhelming advantage, proving highly valuable as an adaptable foundation model for low-resource settings.

### V-C Computation Time
Inference for a single pose (Best of 16) takes about 3.5 ms, and DLS refinement takes about 5 ms. Moreover, batching is extremely efficient: processing 512 poses together drops per-pose inference time to just 0.16 ms. This is ideal for applications like motion planning where large volumes of IK queries must be solved at once.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: toward a foundation model that operates any robot
sections.summary: MorphIK is a breakthrough neural IK solver that generalizes to unseen robots by conditioning on morphology. Combining fast parallel sampling with ultra-high precision via DLS, it takes a major step toward practical IK foundation models.
sections.details:
This paper presented MorphIK, which embeds robot kinematic morphology using a Transformer and generates diverse IK solutions with Flow Matching. Despite being trained purely on synthetic procedural data, it generalized zero-shot to unknown real robots with 6 to 9 DoFs.

The raw model alone produces practical initial poses with errors around 4% of arm length (~5 cm), and adding just 3 steps of DLS optimization yields ultra-high precision in the 0.1 mm range. Furthermore, it demonstrated the ability to thoroughly explore null spaces via GPU parallelism, as well as foundation model potential where precision jumps after just 1 second of fine-tuning.

For future work, the authors highlight exploring how learned morphology embeddings can transfer to other tasks like motion planning or dynamics estimation, and moving toward a fully DoF-invariant architecture by replacing the output layer with a Transformer-based design to handle variable DoFs directly.

takeaways: Unified Geometric Representation: Absorbing URDF variation into a screw-axis-based "canonical representation" is the key to feeding robot morphology into a Transformer.
Power of Synthetic Data: Training on deliberately harsh random robots—with more singularities and harder kinematics than real arms—enables robust zero-shot generalization to real hardware.

Best Mix of AI and Classical Control: The most practical approach pairs neural generative models (Flow Matching) for global discovery and null-space sampling with DLS (local optimization) for a few polish steps.

Second-Scale Fine-Tuning: When specializing a general model to a single arm, starting from a pretrained model reaches practical accuracy in just dozens of steps (about 1 second), far outperforming training from scratch.
limitations: It uses fixed-length padding up to 9 DoFs, so it cannot be directly applied to robots with 10 or more DoFs or branching tree structures (such as multi-fingered hands).
Obstacle environments were not considered during training, meaning collision checking against the environment must be verified and filtered separately by a motion planner.

The 8–9 DoF models used in real-world evaluations were pseudo-configurations created by appending a wrist to existing arms; validation on integrated, custom ultra-high-DoF manipulators remains limited.
